prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- President-elect Barack Obama visited military personnel and their families enjoying Christmas dinner at a Marine Corps base in Hawaii Thursday during his holiday vacation. President-elect Obama shakes hands with troops having Christmas dinner at a military base in Hawaii. Obama went to Marine Corps Base Hawaii Kaneohe Bay on Oahu where he mingled with Marines and sailors. Obama and the troops also had a traditional dinner including turkey, roast beef, ham and trimmings. Obama, dressed casually in a blue polo shirt and dark khaki trousers, chatted casually, shook hands and posed for photos with men and women in the dining hall, which had been decorated with Christmas trees and Santa figurines. Shortly before Obama entered the room, a Marine shouted to the crowd scattered across 25 tables, "You need to take you seats, the president-elect is going to be coming." Obama, who spent about an hour at the Marine base, worked his way around the room, table by table. "Just wanted to say, 'Hi, hey guys,'" Obama said at one point while reporters were allowed in the room. "Hey guys, Merry Christmas," he said to another group. Obama also highlighted the service of the country's military men and women now overseas in a holiday message to be broadcast on radio this Saturday. "As we celebrate this joyous time of year, our thoughts turn to the brave men and women who serve our country far from home," he said in the message, which was posted online Wednesday. "Their extraordinary and selfless sacrifice is an inspiration to us all, and part of the unbroken line of heroism that has made our freedom and prosperity possible for over two centuries."   Watch Obama's holiday message » . More than 140,000 soldiers are currently serving in Iraq, as well as roughly 30,000 in Afghanistan. In the broadcast message, Obama also called on Americans to "renew a sense of common purpose and shared citizenship." "These are also tough times for many Americans struggling in our sluggish economy," he said. "Now, more than ever, we must rededicate ourselves to the notion that we share a common destiny as Americans -- that I am my brother's keeper, I am my sister's keeper. ... We must all do our part to serve one another; to seek new ideas and new innovation; and to start a new chapter for our great country." Obama said that notion "will guide my administration in the New Year. If the American people come together and put their shoulder to the wheel of history, then I know that we can put our people back to work ... and reach the promise of a brighter day."

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** President-elect Barack Obama visited military personnel and their families as they enjoyed Christmas dinner Thursday at a Marine Corps base in Hawaii, where he is spending the holidays.

At Marine Corps Base Hawaii Kaneohe Bay on Oahu, Obama mingled with Marines and sailors, shaking hands with troops and joining them for a traditional dinner of turkey, roast beef, ham and trimmings.

Dressed casually in a blue polo shirt and dark khaki trousers, Obama chatted with service members and posed for photographs with men and women in the dining hall, which was decorated with Christmas trees and Santa figurines.

Shortly before Obama entered, a Marine called out to the crowd spread across 25 tables: “You need to take your seats; the president-elect is going to be coming.”

Obama spent about an hour at the base, making his way around the room table by table.

“Just wanted to say, ‘Hi, hey guys,’” Obama said at one point while reporters were allowed inside. “Hey guys, Merry Christmas,” he told another group.

Obama also honored the service of U.S. military personnel stationed overseas in a holiday message scheduled to be broadcast on radio Saturday.

“As we celebrate this joyous time of year, our thoughts turn to the brave men and women who serve our country far from home,” he said in the message, which was posted online Wednesday. “Their extraordinary and selfless sacrifice is an inspiration to us all, and part of the unbroken line of heroism that has made our freedom and prosperity possible for over two centuries.”

**Watch Obama’s holiday message »**

More than 140,000 troops are currently serving in Iraq, along with roughly 30,000 in Afghanistan.

In the broadcast message, Obama also called on Americans to “renew a sense of common purpose and shared citizenship.”

“These are also tough times for many Americans struggling in our sluggish economy,” he said. “Now, more than ever, we must rededicate ourselves to the notion that we share a common destiny as Americans — that I am my brother’s keeper, I am my sister’s keeper. ... We must all do our part to serve one another; to seek new ideas and new innovation; and to start a new chapter for our great country.”

Obama said that principle “will guide my administration in the New Year. If the American people come together and put their shoulder to the wheel of history, then I know that we can put our people back to work ... and reach the promise of a brighter day.”
outputs.L2:
During his Christmas vacation in Hawaii on Thursday, President-elect Barack Obama stopped by Marine Corps Base Hawaii at Kaneohe Bay on Oahu to visit service members and their families as they ate their holiday meal.

Wearing a blue polo shirt and dark khaki pants, Obama moved among the Marines and sailors in the dining hall, speaking with them, shaking hands and posing for photographs. The room, decorated with Christmas trees and Santa Claus figures, contained 25 tables. Shortly before his arrival, a Marine told those gathered to sit down because the president-elect was about to enter.

Obama spent approximately an hour at the base, making his way from one table to the next. While reporters were present, he greeted one group by explaining that he simply wanted to stop in and say hello. At another table, he wished the service members a merry Christmas.

Obama and the troops shared a customary Christmas dinner featuring turkey, roast beef, ham and accompanying side dishes.

He also honored U.S. military personnel stationed abroad in a holiday radio address scheduled to air Saturday and posted online Wednesday. In the message, Obama said that, during the festive season, Americans were thinking of the courageous men and women serving their country far from their homes. He described their remarkable, selfless sacrifices as an inspiration and as part of a continuous tradition of heroism that had sustained the nation’s freedom and prosperity for more than 200 years.

At the time, over 140,000 U.S. troops were serving in Iraq, while about 30,000 were deployed in Afghanistan.

In the same address, Obama urged Americans to restore a shared sense of national purpose and civic responsibility. He acknowledged that many people were facing hardship because of the weak economy and said the country needed, more than ever, to recommit to the belief that all Americans share the same future and have a responsibility to care for one another.

He called on citizens to help each other, pursue fresh ideas and innovations, and begin a new chapter in the nation’s history. Obama said those principles would shape his administration in the coming year. He added that if Americans united and applied themselves to changing the course of history, the country could put people back to work and move toward the promise of better days.

Obama, who was vacationing with his family on Oahu, moved through the dining hall shaking hands, posing for photographs, and thanking military personnel for their service.

The visit highlighted the sacrifices made by members of the armed forces and by families separated from loved ones deployed overseas. Obama acknowledged that many troops were spending the holiday far from home, particularly those serving in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In a holiday radio message, the president-elect paid tribute to those service members and emphasized the nation’s obligation to support them and their families. He said their service reflected values shared by Americans across political, religious, and regional lines.

Obama also addressed the economic difficulties confronting the country. With many families struggling because of job losses, financial uncertainty, and the growing recession, he urged Americans to draw strength from one another and to remember their responsibilities as citizens.

The challenges ahead, he said, would require more than action from government alone. They would also demand renewed common purpose, mutual sacrifice, and a willingness to work together. By embracing that spirit of shared citizenship, Obama argued, Americans could overcome the economic crisis and build a stronger future.

# Obama visits Marines, sailors during Christmas dinner in Hawaii

**KANEOHE BAY, Hawaii (CNN) —** President-elect Barack Obama spent part of Christmas Day 2008 greeting Marines, sailors and their families during dinner at Marine Corps Base Hawaii.

Obama visited Anderson Hall at the Kaneohe Bay installation, moving through the dining facility to shake hands, pose for photographs and thank service members for their work. The unannounced stop came as troops and their families gathered for a traditional Christmas meal.

The president-elect, who was vacationing with his family in his native Hawaii, did not deliver a formal speech. His visit was brief and largely informal, with service members lining up for a chance to meet the incoming commander in chief.

The base is home to thousands of Marines, sailors and their families, including personnel who had served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Obama’s Christmas appearance offered an early glimpse of his coming role as commander in chief. He was scheduled to be sworn in as the 44th president of the United States on January 20, 2009, inheriting two ongoing wars and major decisions about troop deployments overseas.

The visit was one of the few public events during Obama’s holiday stay in Hawaii.

“We know that many of you are missing your families,” Obama told the troops. “The American people are thinking of you, and we are grateful for your service.”

Obama, who was spending the holiday with his family in Hawaii, visited the base’s dining hall to greet military personnel, pose for photographs and offer Christmas wishes. He said the country owed a special debt to Americans serving overseas and to the families supporting them at home.

counterfactuals.output:
# Obama greets troops, families during holiday visit to Marine dining hall

**KANEOHE BAY, Hawaii (CNN)** — President-elect Barack Obama spent about an hour greeting U.S. service members and their families at a festively decorated Marine Corps dining hall Thursday, offering holiday wishes as American troops remained deployed in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Obama, vacationing with his family in his native Hawaii, visited Anderson Hall at Marine Corps Base Hawaii in Kaneohe Bay. The dining facility was decorated for Christmas, providing a holiday setting for troops and relatives gathered for a meal far from extended family members — and, for some, while loved ones served overseas.

Moving through the hall, Obama shook hands, posed for photographs and spoke briefly with Marines, sailors and military families. The visit was informal, with the president-elect spending much of his time in one-on-one conversations rather than delivering a formal speech.

The stop came less than a month before Obama was to take office and assume responsibility for two wars. Tens of thousands of U.S. troops remained in Afghanistan, where violence had intensified, while a much larger American force was still stationed in Iraq despite improving security conditions and plans for a gradual withdrawal.

Obama campaigned on a pledge to end the war in Iraq responsibly and to place greater emphasis on Afghanistan, which he described as a central front in the fight against al Qaeda and its allies. His incoming administration was expected to review military strategy, troop levels and the demands placed on service members who had endured repeated deployments.

Those decisions would carry immediate consequences for many of the families Obama met in Hawaii. Years of war had required extended tours, shortened time at home and multiple separations for troops from across the armed services.

Obama has repeatedly said the burden of war should not fall only on military families. In a holiday message, he called on Americans to embrace a broader sense of shared citizenship, arguing that national service includes supporting troops, helping neighbors and accepting common responsibility for the country’s future.

“America is a family,” Obama said in the message, emphasizing obligations that extend beyond politics and government. He urged Americans to remember those serving abroad, as well as their spouses, children and parents at home.

The theme echoed a central idea of Obama’s presidential campaign: that citizenship requires participation and sacrifice, not simply the expectation that government or the military will solve national problems. He has called for expanded opportunities for civilian service and greater support for veterans and military families.

At the Marine dining hall, that message took a personal form. Obama paused to speak with children, thanked service members and listened as families described their experiences. The visit gave troops an opportunity to meet the incoming commander in chief before he began making decisions about deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Obama has said he intends to consult military commanders and national security advisers before setting final timelines. He has also emphasized the need to care for wounded troops, improve veterans’ services and provide military families with better access to health care, education and other assistance.

The president-elect did not use the Christmas appearance to announce policy. Instead, the hourlong visit focused on recognition and gratitude, with Obama acknowledging the men and women whose service would shape some of the most difficult choices of his presidency.

As troops and their families continued their holiday meal beneath seasonal decorations, Obama’s stop highlighted the contrast between celebrations at home and the realities of wars thousands of miles away — conflicts he would soon inherit as president and commander in chief.
